questions.t: In AutoGen's conversation programming, each agent auto-replies until a termination condition is met, so the control flow emerges from the conversation itself.
questions.f: In AutoGen's conversation programming, each agent replies only along edges of a state graph defined in advance, so the control flow is fixed before the conversation.
questions.x: A single opening message can drive a long multi-agent exchange, with control steered by system messages or custom Python reply functions. Explicit state graphs are the approach of LangGraph, the main alternative design.

questions.topic: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
questions.t: In the 2023 AutoGen paper, a GPT-4-based AutoGen setup solved 52.5% of 120 level-5 MATH problems, against 30.0% for plain GPT-4.
questions.f: In the 2023 AutoGen paper, a GPT-4-based AutoGen setup solved 52.5% of 120 level-5 MATH problems, against 48.3% for plain GPT-4.
questions.x: Letting an assistant agent write code and a proxy agent run it gave GPT-4 a feedback loop it lacks when answering directly. The 48.33% figure was ChatGPT with Code Interpreter, a closer competitor that also executes code.

questions.topic: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
questions.t: Microsoft Agent Framework is the direct successor to both AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, combining AutoGen's agent abstractions with Semantic Kernel's enterprise features.
questions.f: Microsoft Agent Framework is the direct successor to both AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, combining Semantic Kernel's agent abstractions with AutoGen's enterprise features.
questions.x: The AutoGen repository is archived and points new users to Agent Framework, built by the same teams. It also adds explicit workflows for controlling multi-agent execution paths, which AutoGen's emergent conversations lacked.

questions.t: In ILSVRC-2012, AlexNet's seven-network ensemble scored 15.3% top-5 test error, against 26.2% for the second-best entry.
questions.f: In ILSVRC-2012, AlexNet's seven-network ensemble scored 15.3% top-5 test error, against 17.0% for the second-best entry.
questions.x: The point of the 2012 result was the size of the gap: an error rate more than ten points below the hand-engineered runner-up is what convinced computer vision to switch to deep learning. By 2014 nearly every top entry used convolutional networks.

questions.t: ImageNet was introduced at CVPR 2009 by Jia Deng, Li Fei-Fei and colleagues, who organized its images under WordNet's noun hierarchy.
questions.f: ImageNet was introduced at CVPR 2012 by Alex Krizhevsky, Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues, who organized its images under WordNet's noun hierarchy.
questions.x: The dataset came three years before the model: Deng, Fei-Fei and colleagues built it, labeling with crowd workers, and the Toronto team behind AlexNet used it. Its WordNet roots later drew criticism for the person categories it inherited.

questions.t: AlexNet's authors found that removing any single convolutional layer hurt accuracy, even though each held at most 1% of the parameters, an early sign that depth itself mattered.
questions.f: AlexNet's authors found that removing any single convolutional layer barely changed accuracy, since each held at most 1% of the parameters, an early sign that width mattered more than depth.
questions.x: Most of AlexNet's parameters sat in its fully connected layers, so the convolutional layers looked cheap. That losing even one still cost accuracy suggested the stack of learned feature levels, not raw parameter count, was doing the work.

questions.t: High-bandwidth memory (HBM) gets its bandwidth from a very wide interface of short in-package wires running at modest per-pin speeds.
questions.f: High-bandwidth memory (HBM) gets its bandwidth from a narrow interface of short in-package wires running at very high per-pin speeds.
questions.x: HBM stacks DRAM dies joined by through-silicon vias and sits beside the processor on an interposer, exposing 1,024 bits per stack in early generations. Width, not per-pin speed, is the trick; the narrow, fast bus describes conventional board-mounted memory such as GDDR.

questions.t: High-bandwidth memory first reached the market in 2015, in AMD's Fiji graphics processors built with memory partner SK hynix.
questions.f: High-bandwidth memory first reached the market in 2018, in AMD's Fiji graphics processors built with memory partner SK hynix.
questions.x: AMD's Radeon R9 Fury family launched HBM in 2015, replacing GDDR5 and claiming about four times the bandwidth per watt. 2018 is when JEDEC's JESD235B update raised per-pin rates, a revision of an already shipping standard.

questions.t: A 2024 'memory wall' analysis estimated that peak server FLOPS grew about 3.0x every two years over two decades, while DRAM bandwidth grew only about 1.6x.
questions.f: A 2024 'memory wall' analysis estimated that DRAM bandwidth grew about 3.0x every two years over two decades, while peak server FLOPS grew only about 1.6x.
questions.x: Gholami and colleagues found compute outpacing memory bandwidth, which is why many AI workloads, especially LLM decoding, are limited by bytes moved rather than arithmetic. HBM narrows that gap but has not closed it.

questions.t: In 1989 George Cybenko proved that a single hidden layer of continuous sigmoidal units can approximate any continuous function on the unit cube arbitrarily well.
questions.f: In 1989 George Cybenko proved that a single hidden layer of linear units can approximate any continuous function on the unit cube arbitrarily well.
questions.x: The nonlinearity is what makes it work: sums of sigmoids can bend into any continuous shape, while linear units only ever add up to a linear map. Hornik, Stinchcombe and White published a closely related result the same year.

questions.t: The universal approximation theorem is an existence result: it shows suitable weights exist but bounds neither the number of hidden units needed nor whether training will find them.
questions.f: The universal approximation theorem is a constructive result: it gives the suitable weights and bounds both the number of hidden units needed and whether training will find them.
questions.x: Cybenko's proof works by contradiction and places no limit on width or weight size. Lecture notes add that worst-case size grows exponentially with input dimension and that training is non-convex, so expressive power alone doesn't explain why networks learn well.

questions.t: Lu and colleagues (NeurIPS 2017) showed ReLU networks of width n + 4 for n inputs are universal approximators as depth grows, while networks of width at most n generally are not.
questions.f: Lu and colleagues (NeurIPS 2017) showed ReLU networks of width n for n inputs are universal approximators as depth grows, while networks of width at most n − 4 generally are not.
questions.x: The classical theorems fix depth at one hidden layer and let width grow; this is the mirror image, fixing width and letting depth grow. The sharp jump between width n and n + 4 is a phase transition in what narrow deep networks can represent.

questions.t: Compute governance treats compute as a policy lever because, unlike data and algorithms, its use is detectable, access is excludable, it is quantifiable and its supply chain is concentrated.
questions.f: Compute governance treats data as a policy lever because, unlike compute and algorithms, its use is detectable, access is excludable, it is quantifiable and its supply chain is concentrated.
questions.x: Sastry, Heim and co-authors argued in 2024 that data and algorithms are easy to copy and hard to observe, whereas chips are physical, countable and made by very few producers. That is what makes reporting, allocation and export controls workable.

questions.t: A 2024 paper reported training compute for notable ML systems doubling about every six months, while GPU price-performance doubled only every two to two-and-a-half years.
questions.f: A 2024 paper reported training compute for notable ML systems doubling about every two years, while GPU price-performance doubled roughly every six months.
questions.x: Because compute grew far faster than chips got cheaper, most of the growth came from bigger clusters and more spending. That spending makes large training runs visible, which is what gives compute governance its leverage.

questions.t: Sara Hooker argues fixed training-compute thresholds are shortsighted because the link between compute and risk is uncertain and shifting.
questions.f: Sara Hooker argues fixed training-compute thresholds are reliable because the link between compute and risk is predictable and stable.
questions.x: Compute is only a good proxy for risk while capability rises predictably with scale, the scaling-law assumption Hooker challenges. Efficiency gains also erode any fixed cut-off, and small narrow models can still be dangerous.

questions.topic: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
questions.t: FlashAttention computes exact attention, giving the same result as standard attention, so it is a drop-in speedup rather than a modelling change.
questions.f: FlashAttention computes a low-rank approximation of attention, giving a slightly different result, so it is a modelling change rather than a drop-in speedup.
questions.x: Its gains come from moving fewer bytes between GPU high-bandwidth memory and on-chip SRAM, not from approximating. Sparse and low-rank methods trade accuracy for speed; FlashAttention keeps the maths identical, which is why it spread so quickly.

questions.topic: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
questions.t: FlashAttention keeps a running row maximum and sum of exponentials, rescaling partial outputs per block, so it never stores the N×N score matrix.
questions.f: FlashAttention writes the N×N score matrix to high-bandwidth memory once, then reads it back in blocks to apply softmax and multiply by V.
questions.x: Softmax normally needs a whole row before normalising, which forces naive attention to write and reread the score matrix. The 'online softmax' trick fixes the normalisation as blocks arrive, so the full computation fuses into one kernel with memory linear in sequence length.

questions.topic: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
questions.t: In 2023 FlashAttention-2 reached 50–73% of an A100's peak FLOPs/s, up from 25–40% for the original FlashAttention.
questions.f: In 2023 FlashAttention-2 reached 25–40% of an A100's peak FLOPs/s, up from 10–20% for the original FlashAttention.
questions.x: FlashAttention-2 roughly doubled speed by cutting non-matmul work, parallelising over sequence length and splitting work across warps. Utilisation then fell again on newer hardware, which is why FlashAttention-3 and -4 were redesigned for Hopper and Blackwell.

questions.t: Karl Pearson (1901) derived PCA as fitting the closest lines and planes to a cloud of points; Harold Hotelling (1933) derived it as the projection that maximises variance.
questions.f: Harold Hotelling (1901) derived PCA as fitting the closest lines and planes to a cloud of points; Karl Pearson (1933) derived it as the projection that maximises variance.
questions.x: Pearson's geometric view minimises squared reconstruction error, and Hotelling's statistical view maximises projected variance. The two derivations give the same components, which is why PCA can be explained either way.

questions.t: PCA keeps the covariance eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues, because each eigenvalue is the variance captured along that component.
questions.f: PCA keeps the covariance eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues, because each eigenvalue is the variance captured along that component.
questions.x: Sorting by eigenvalue ranks directions by how much spread they hold, so the discarded eigenvalues add up to exactly the variance the projection throws away. For high-dimensional data, implementations get the same directions from an SVD of the centred data instead.

questions.t: Scikit-learn's PCA centres each feature but doesn't scale it, so variables measured on large scales dominate the components unless you rescale them first.
questions.f: Scikit-learn's PCA centres each feature and scales it to unit variance, so variables measured on large scales can't dominate the components even if you skip rescaling.
questions.x: Because PCA chases variance, a feature in large units looks important simply because its numbers are big. Whether to standardise is a real modelling choice; NIST's tutorial standardises and works from the correlation matrix instead.

questions.t: Self-Refine prompts one LLM to draft an answer, critique it and rewrite it, and the refine prompt carries the history of earlier drafts and critiques.
questions.f: Self-Refine trains a separate critic model to critique a generator LLM's draft, and the refine prompt carries only the current draft and its critique.
questions.x: All three roles are the same frozen model set up with few-shot prompts, so the method needs no training data or weight updates. Keeping the full history lets the model avoid repeating mistakes it already made in earlier rounds.

questions.t: In the 2023 Self-Refine paper, GPT-4's dialogue response score rose from 25.4 to 74.6, while its GSM8K math score barely moved, from 92.9 to 93.1.
questions.f: In the 2023 Self-Refine paper, GPT-4's GSM8K math score rose from 25.4 to 74.6, while its dialogue response score barely moved, from 92.9 to 93.1.
questions.x: Open-ended tasks with many acceptable answers benefited most from critique and rewriting. On math the model rarely noticed its own errors, judging most flawed solutions as fine, so self-feedback had little to work with.

questions.t: Huang et al. argued Self-Refine's CommonGen-Hard gains partly came from the feedback prompt adding a requirement the first prompt left out; stating it up front scored higher.
questions.f: Huang et al. argued Self-Refine's CommonGen-Hard gains partly came from the feedback prompt adding a requirement the first prompt left out; stating it up front scored lower.
questions.x: The requirement to use every concept was only spelled out at the feedback step, so revision looked better than a fairly written first prompt. A plain prompt that stated it scored 81.8 against Self-Refine's 75.1, a reminder to compare self-correction loops with simply improving the initial prompt.

questions.t: Thompson sampling draws one plausible model from its posterior and acts optimally for that sample, so each action is tried in proportion to the chance it is best.
questions.f: Thompson sampling adds a confidence bonus to each action's estimate and picks the highest total, so each action is tried in proportion to the chance it is best.
questions.x: Thompson sampling explores through randomness in its beliefs: uncertain actions sometimes win the posterior draw. Adding a shrinking confidence bonus to each estimate is the upper confidence bound (UCB) approach, which explores through optimism rather than sampling.

questions.t: Optimistic initial values push even a greedy learner to try every action early on, but the effect fades, so they do not help in nonstationary problems.
questions.f: Optimistic initial values push even a greedy learner to try every action early on, and the effect persists, so they suit nonstationary problems well.
questions.x: Starting every estimate too high means early rewards disappoint, so the learner keeps moving on to untried actions. Once the estimates settle the push to explore is gone, which is why the trick fails when the best action changes over time and exploration must restart.

questions.t: On Sutton and Barto's 10-armed testbed, ε = 0.1 found the best arm sooner, while ε = 0.01 learned more slowly but did better in the long run.
questions.f: On Sutton and Barto's 10-armed testbed, ε = 0.01 found the best arm sooner, while ε = 0.1 learned more slowly but did better in the long run.
questions.x: More random exploration discovers the best arm faster but keeps wasting a tenth of the choices on random arms forever. A smaller ε explores slowly, yet once it finds the best arm it exploits it almost all the time, so it pulls ahead later. A purely greedy learner often got stuck on a worse arm.

questions.t: Word2vec gives each vocabulary word one fixed vector whatever sentence it appears in, so it cannot separate the river and the money senses of "bank".
questions.f: Word2vec gives each vocabulary word a new vector in every sentence it appears in, so it can separate the river and the money senses of "bank".
questions.x: Word2vec embeddings are static: one vector per word type, blending all its senses. Producing a different vector per occurrence is what contextual encoders such as BERT do, which is why they replaced static vectors in most modern systems.

questions.t: Word2vec's negative sampling draws noise words from the unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power, which slightly raises how often rare words are picked as negatives.
questions.f: Word2vec's negative sampling draws noise words from the unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power, which slightly raises how often frequent words are picked as negatives.
questions.x: Negative sampling turns training into telling real word-context pairs from k noise words, avoiding a full softmax over the vocabulary. Raising frequencies to 0.75 flattens the distribution, so rare words get a bit more of the probability mass and frequent ones a bit less.

questions.t: Levy and Goldberg showed skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorises a word-context matrix of pointwise mutual information shifted by a constant.
questions.f: Levy and Goldberg showed skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorises a term-document matrix of tf-idf weights shifted by a constant.
questions.x: This result tied word2vec back to count-based distributional methods built on PMI. An exact SVD of that matrix could match it on word similarity, though skip-gram stayed ahead on analogies; tf-idf weights term-document counts and is a different, sparse scheme.

questions.t: In Gao, Schulman and Hilton's study of RLHF overoptimization, larger proxy reward models reached higher gold scores and suffered less overoptimization.
questions.f: In Gao, Schulman and Hilton's study of RLHF overoptimization, smaller proxy reward models reached higher gold scores and suffered less overoptimization.
questions.x: A larger reward model is a better proxy for human judgement, so a policy can push further against it before the true (gold) score turns down. The benefit scaled smoothly with parameter count, which makes reward-model size a practical lever against reward hacking in RLHF, though not a cure.

questions.t: OpenAI researchers found that folding a chain-of-thought monitor into the training reward, under heavy optimisation pressure, taught agents to hide their intent while still reward hacking.
questions.f: OpenAI researchers found that folding a chain-of-thought monitor into the training reward, under heavy optimisation pressure, taught agents to stop reward hacking and state their intent openly.
questions.x: Reading the chain of thought made hacks much easier to catch, but penalising what the monitor saw gave the agent a reason to clean up its reasoning rather than its behaviour. That is why the authors suggest a 'monitorability tax': leave the chain of thought unoptimised so it stays useful for oversight.

questions.t: Anthropic's inoculation prompting tells a model during training that reward hacking is acceptable in that context, which largely stopped the hacking from spreading into broader misalignment.
questions.f: Anthropic's inoculation prompting tells a model during training that reward hacking is forbidden in that context, which largely stopped the hacking from spreading into broader misalignment.
questions.x: Anthropic saw a model that learned to game coding tests go on to sabotage safety code and fake alignment, even though standard safety training made it look fine in chat. Counterintuitively, permitting the hack in context removed that spillover, and Anthropic says it now uses the technique.

questions.t: In classic fine-tuning, the copied pretrained layers get a small learning rate, while the new randomly initialised output layer gets a larger one.
questions.f: In classic fine-tuning, the copied pretrained layers get a large learning rate, while the new randomly initialised output layer gets a smaller one.
questions.x: The copied layers already hold useful features, so big updates would mostly damage them, while the new head starts from scratch and must move a long way. Dive into Deep Learning's example gives the head ten times the backbone's learning rate.

questions.t: Kumar et al. (ICLR 2022) found full fine-tuning beat linear probing in distribution but did worse out of distribution, and probing first then fine-tuning recovered much of the gap.
questions.f: Kumar et al. (ICLR 2022) found full fine-tuning beat linear probing out of distribution but did worse in distribution, and probing first then fine-tuning recovered much of the gap.
questions.x: While a random head is still being learned, its noisy gradients distort the pretrained lower layers, which hurts robustness to distribution shift. Fitting a linear probe first (LP-FT) gives the head a sensible start, so fine-tuning changes the features less.

questions.t: In 2018, ULMFiT fine-tuned with only 100 labelled examples matched a text classifier trained from scratch on 100 times more data.
questions.f: In 2018, ULMFiT fine-tuned with only 100 labelled examples matched a text classifier trained from scratch on 10 times more data.
questions.x: Howard and Ruder's result showed how much labelled data a pretrained language model saves, which helped make pretrain-then-fine-tune the default recipe in NLP. The saving was a hundredfold, not tenfold.

questions.t: Decoder-only Transformers apply a causal mask that sets attention scores for future positions to negative infinity, so each token can attend only to earlier tokens.
questions.f: Encoder-only Transformers apply a causal mask that sets attention scores for future positions to negative infinity, so each token can attend only to earlier tokens.
questions.x: The causal mask is what makes a decoder-only model a left-to-right generator that can still train on all positions in parallel. Encoder-only models such as BERT use no mask, so every token sees both left and right context.

questions.t: Xiong et al. (2020) showed that Post-LN Transformers have large gradients near the output at initialization, so they need learning-rate warm-up, while Pre-LN ones can train without it.
questions.f: Xiong et al. (2020) showed that Pre-LN Transformers have large gradients near the output at initialization, so they need learning-rate warm-up, while Post-LN ones can train without it.
questions.x: The original Transformer normalized after each residual addition (Post-LN). Moving layer normalization inside the residual branch (Pre-LN) keeps gradients well behaved, which is why later models such as LLaMA normalize sub-layer inputs.

questions.t: As of 2026, almost no large Transformer language models use anything but standard quadratic attention, because cheaper attention variants often underperform at scale.
questions.f: As of 2026, most large Transformer language models have replaced standard quadratic attention, because cheaper attention variants usually match it at scale.
questions.x: Self-attention compares every pair of positions, so cost grows with the square of sequence length and limits the context window. Many sub-quadratic variants exist, but Stanford's CS224N notes they rarely survive at scale, so better long-context designs remain an open question.

questions.t: COCO's primary detection score averages precision over ten IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95, while PASCAL VOC counted a detection correct at a single 50% IoU threshold.
questions.f: COCO's primary detection score counts a detection correct at a single 50% IoU threshold, while PASCAL VOC averaged precision over ten IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95.
questions.x: Intersection over union (IoU) measures how well a predicted box overlaps the true one. VOC's 50% bar was deliberately lenient, so one number hid poor localization; COCO's averaging over stricter thresholds rewards boxes that fit tightly.

questions.t: DETR trains with a bipartite-matching loss that assigns each object exactly one prediction, which lets it drop non-maximum suppression and hand-built anchors.
questions.f: DETR trains with an anchor-matching loss that assigns each object several predictions, which means it still relies on non-maximum suppression and hand-built anchors.
questions.x: Conventional detectors let many candidates fire on one object and prune the duplicates afterwards with non-maximum suppression. DETR instead treats detection as set prediction from a fixed set of learned object queries, so duplicates are penalised during training rather than removed after it.

questions.t: In 2014 Girshick, Donahue, Darrell and Malik's R-CNN ran a convolutional network on region proposals and raised PASCAL VOC 2012 mAP by over 30% relative to the prior best.
questions.f: In 2014 Ren, He, Girshick and Sun's R-CNN ran a convolutional network on region proposals and raised PASCAL VOC 2012 mAP by over 30% relative to the prior best.
questions.x: R-CNN broke a plateau of hand-engineered feature pipelines and showed that an ImageNet-pretrained network fine-tuned on scarce detection data works well. Ren, He, Girshick and Sun wrote the later Faster R-CNN paper, which kept Girshick but changed the rest of the team.

questions.t: Oren et al.'s contamination test relies on a clean model finding every ordering of a benchmark's examples equally likely, so a preference for the published order signals memorisation.
questions.f: Oren et al.'s contamination test relies on a clean model preferring the published ordering of a benchmark's examples, so equal likelihood across shuffles signals memorisation.
questions.x: A model that never saw the test set has no reason to favour the order the examples were published in. If it does, it has probably read that file, and because the test only needs output probabilities it works on black-box models with exact false-positive guarantees.

questions.t: On GSM1k, a fresh set matched to GSM8K, some leading models scored up to 8% lower, though many frontier models showed little sign of overfitting (NeurIPS 2024).
questions.f: On GSM1k, a fresh set matched to GSM8K, some leading models scored up to 8% higher, though many frontier models showed little sign of overfitting (NeurIPS 2024).
questions.x: Rebuilding a benchmark from scratch and comparing is the clearest way to measure contamination's effect: a drop on unseen but equivalent problems means the old score was inflated. The result was mixed, with some model families overfit and many frontier models not.

questions.t: LiveBench limits contamination by drawing questions from recent competitions, arXiv papers and news, refreshing them monthly and scoring against objective answers.
questions.f: LiveBench limits contamination by drawing questions from recent competitions, arXiv papers and news, refreshing them monthly and scoring them with LLM judges.
questions.x: Fresh questions are unlikely to be in any model's training data yet, and objective answers avoid the biases of LLM judges or crowdworkers. Even so, its authors softened the claim from 'contamination-free' to 'contamination-limited'.

questions.topic: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
questions.t: Generative agents rank memories by summing recency, importance and relevance, where importance is a 1–10 rating the LLM gives each memory when it is stored.
questions.f: Generative agents rank memories by summing recency, importance and relevance, where importance is the cosine similarity between the memory's embedding and the current query.
questions.x: Embedding similarity to the query is the relevance score; importance separates mundane events from poignant ones. Combining the three lets an agent recall what is recent, significant and on-topic rather than just the closest match.

questions.topic: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
questions.t: In generative agents, a reflection is a higher-level insight written about recent memories and stored back in the memory stream, so later reflections can build on it.
questions.f: In generative agents, a reflection is a higher-level summary that replaces recent memories in the memory stream, so later reflections can only use the summary.
questions.x: Reflections cite the memories that support them and sit alongside raw observations, forming trees of increasingly abstract beliefs. They are triggered when the summed importance of recent events passes a threshold, a few times per simulated day.

questions.topic: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
questions.t: In believability interviews, the full generative-agent architecture outranked human crowdworkers role-playing the agents, and the version without memory, reflection or planning ranked lowest.
questions.f: In believability interviews, human crowdworkers role-playing the agents outranked the full generative-agent architecture, and the version without memory, reflection or planning ranked lowest.
questions.x: The ablations show each component adds believability, with removing reflection alone already lowering the ranking. The authors caution the crowdworkers were not meant to represent expert human performance, so this is not a claim of beating people in general.

questions.t: Joseph Weizenbaum of MIT described ELIZA, a program for typed conversation in English, in Communications of the ACM in 1966.
questions.f: Joseph Weizenbaum of MIT described ELIZA, a program for typed conversation in English, in Communications of the ACM in 1976.
questions.x: ELIZA dates to 1966 and ran on MIT's time-sharing system. 1976 is the year of Weizenbaum's book Computer Power and Human Reason, in which he warned against handing machines choices that are properly human.

questions.t: When ELIZA found several script keywords in an input, a higher-ranked keyword displaced a lower-ranked one, and its rules then built the reply.
questions.f: When ELIZA found several script keywords in an input, the first keyword found displaced any later ones, and its rules then built the reply.
questions.x: Each keyword in the script carries a rank, so the most important one wins regardless of position. A decomposition rule then splits the input around it and a reassembly rule rebuilds the fragments, swapping pronouns: pattern matching on surface text, not understanding.

questions.t: Weizenbaum used a Rogerian psychotherapist for ELIZA's DOCTOR script because such an interviewer can seem to know almost nothing about the world.
questions.f: Weizenbaum used a Rogerian psychotherapist for ELIZA's DOCTOR script because such an interviewer is expected to know a great deal about the world.
questions.x: A therapist who reflects questions back hides the program's total lack of knowledge, so users fill in the understanding themselves. That human tendency to read meaning into simple output became known as the ELIZA effect.

questions.t: Before compute APIs such as CUDA arrived, GPGPU programmers stored arrays as textures and wrote their kernels as fragment shaders.
questions.f: Before compute APIs such as CUDA arrived, GPGPU programmers stored arrays in shared memory and wrote their kernels as thread blocks.
questions.x: Early general-purpose GPU work had to disguise computation as graphics, which imposed 2D layouts and made scattered writes awkward. Shared memory, pointers and thread blocks only came with the compute interfaces AMD and NVIDIA shipped in 2006–2007.

questions.t: GPUs hide memory latency by switching among many resident warps, so a kernel launch needs far more threads than the GPU has cores.
questions.f: GPUs hide memory latency with large per-thread caches, so a kernel launch needs about as many threads as the GPU has cores.
questions.x: GPUs trade latency for throughput: while some warps wait on memory, others compute. NVIDIA suggests roughly four times as many thread blocks as streaming multiprocessors; too few threads leave units idle, as in the tail effect of a last partial wave.

questions.t: In NVIDIA's performance guide, a linear layer at batch size 512 is math-limited, while ReLU and layer normalization are memory-limited.
questions.f: In NVIDIA's performance guide, a linear layer at batch size 512 is memory-limited, while ReLU and layer normalization are math-limited.
questions.x: What matters is arithmetic intensity, operations per byte moved. A large-batch matrix multiply reaches about 315 FLOPS per byte, above the GPU's ratio, while elementwise ReLU does about 0.25, so it just waits on memory; that is why peak FLOPS are rarely reached.

questions.t: Because a convolutional layer reuses one kernel at every position, shifting the input image shifts its feature map by the same amount, a property called translation equivariance.
questions.f: Because a convolutional layer reuses one kernel at every position, shifting the input image leaves its feature map unchanged, a property called translation invariance.
questions.x: Weight sharing means a feature detector responds to a pattern wherever it appears, and its response moves with the pattern. It also slashes parameters: a few hundred shared weights instead of about a billion for a dense layer on a megapixel image.

questions.t: Fukushima's 1980 neocognitron learned without labels, whereas LeCun and colleagues later trained convolutional networks end to end with backpropagation.
questions.f: Fukushima's 1980 neocognitron was trained end to end with backpropagation, whereas LeCun and colleagues later trained convolutional networks without labels.
questions.x: The neocognitron supplied the architecture of alternating feature-detecting and pooling-like layers, inspired by simple and complex cells in the visual cortex. Training it with gradients was LeCun's step, and it led to deployed systems such as cheque readers.

questions.t: The 'convolution' in deep-learning libraries is really cross-correlation, without flipping the kernel, and the difference does not matter because the kernel is learned.
questions.f: The 'convolution' in deep-learning libraries is true convolution with a flipped kernel, and the flip matters because cross-correlation would learn different features.
questions.x: Convolution and cross-correlation differ only by flipping the kernel. Since training starts from random weights, a network using cross-correlation simply learns the flipped kernel, so the results are equivalent.

questions.t: Dafoe's AI governance research agenda has three clusters: the technical landscape, AI politics, and ideal governance, which asks what institutions would best ensure beneficial AI.
questions.f: Dafoe's AI governance research agenda has three clusters: the technical landscape, AI politics, and ideal governance, which asks what AI will be able to do and when.
questions.x: Forecasting what AI can do and when belongs to the technical landscape cluster. Ideal governance is the normative part, asking which norms, institutions and systems should steer AI toward beneficial use.

questions.t: Jobin, Ienca and Vayena's review of 84 AI ethics guidelines found convergence on five themes, yet no single principle appeared in every document.
questions.f: Jobin, Ienca and Vayena's review of 84 AI ethics guidelines found convergence on five themes, with transparency appearing in every document.
questions.x: Transparency, justice and fairness, non-maleficence, responsibility and privacy recurred, but none was universal, and authors disagreed on what the terms mean and how to implement them. It is a core piece of evidence for the critique that principles outran enforceable practice.

questions.t: Under the EU AI Act's risk tiers, chatbots carry transparency duties, while recruitment tools are high-risk and must meet data-quality and human-oversight requirements.
questions.f: Under the EU AI Act's risk tiers, recruitment tools carry transparency duties, while chatbots are high-risk and must meet data-quality and human-oversight requirements.
questions.x: The Act scales obligations to the harm a use can cause: decisions about people's jobs or health are high-risk, a chatbot mainly must disclose what it is. Most systems, like spam filters, carry no duties, and practices such as social scoring are banned.

questions.t: Structured pruning removes whole channels, heads or blocks, leaving a smaller dense network, while unstructured pruning zeroes individual weights in an irregular pattern.
questions.f: Unstructured pruning removes whole channels, heads or blocks, leaving a smaller dense network, while structured pruning zeroes individual weights in an irregular pattern.
questions.x: Unstructured pruning reaches the highest sparsity for a given accuracy, but its scattered zeros are hard for hardware to exploit. Structured pruning gives up some sparsity so ordinary dense kernels can run the slimmer model faster.

questions.t: Frankle and Carbin found pruned subnetworks train to comparable accuracy when reset to their original initial weights, but not when freshly reinitialised.
questions.f: Frankle and Carbin found pruned subnetworks train to comparable accuracy when freshly reinitialised, but not when reset to their original initial weights.
questions.x: This lottery ticket result suggests pruning finds favourable initialisations, not just redundant weights. The sparse structure alone is not enough: the same mask with new random weights falls short of the dense network.

questions.t: As of 2021, NVIDIA's 2:4 sparsity doubled A100 peak throughput on paper, yet its measured throughput gain on a sparse ResNeXt-101 was up to about 20%.
questions.f: As of 2021, NVIDIA's 2:4 sparsity doubled A100 peak throughput on paper, and its measured throughput gain on a sparse ResNeXt-101 was the full 2x.
questions.x: In 2:4 sparsity two of every four contiguous weights are zero, which Sparse Tensor Cores can skip. Peak figures still overstate real speedups, a recurring gap between parameter reductions and measured gains in pruning.

questions.t: In supervised learning, a continuous target such as a house price makes the task regression, while a target with a few discrete values makes it classification.
questions.f: In supervised learning, a continuous target such as a house price makes the task classification, while a target with a few discrete values makes it regression.
questions.x: The type of label decides the task: regression predicts a number on a continuous scale, classification picks one of a small set of categories. The choice also shapes the loss, such as squared error for regression and cross-entropy for classification.

questions.t: Fixing a narrower hypothesis class in advance makes empirical risk minimization less prone to overfitting, at the price of a stronger inductive bias.
questions.f: Fixing a wider hypothesis class in advance makes empirical risk minimization less prone to overfitting, at the price of a stronger inductive bias.
questions.x: Unrestricted ERM can pick a predictor that memorises the training set: zero training error, chance-level on new data. Limiting the class blocks such lookup tables, but if the class is too narrow it may miss the true pattern.

questions.t: Leslie Valiant's 1984 paper "A Theory of the Learnable" gave learning a computational footing, the template later called probably approximately correct (PAC) learning.
questions.f: Leslie Valiant's 1994 paper "A Theory of the Learnable" gave learning a computational footing, the template later called probably approximately correct (PAC) learning.
questions.x: Valiant's 1984 Communications of the ACM paper asked a learner to produce, in polynomial time, a rule whose error is small with high probability. That framing underlies the formal theory of supervised learning taught today.

questions.t: Liu et al.'s 2021 survey named the 'pre-train, prompt, and predict' paradigm, in which an input is wrapped in a template whose open slots the language model fills.
questions.f: Brown et al.'s 2020 GPT-3 paper named the 'pre-train, prompt, and predict' paradigm, in which an input is wrapped in a template whose open slots the language model fills.
questions.x: GPT-3 showed in 2020 that tasks could be specified purely in text; Liu and colleagues' survey a year later gave the shift its name. The point is that one pretrained model is steered by templates instead of training a separate supervised model per task.

questions.t: Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE) has an LLM propose candidate instructions, scores each one on training examples, and keeps the best performer.
questions.f: Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE) has humans propose candidate instructions, has an LLM score each one by its fluency, and keeps the best performer.
questions.x: APE treats the instruction as a program to search over, with a model generating candidates and a metric such as training accuracy choosing among them. This reframes prompt writing as optimisation; across 24 tasks its instructions matched or beat human ones on 21.

questions.t: In OpenAI's chat APIs, developer messages take priority over user messages, which OpenAI likens to a function definition and the arguments passed to it.
questions.f: In OpenAI's chat APIs, user messages take priority over developer messages, which OpenAI likens to a function's arguments overriding its definition.
questions.x: Separating roles lets an application fix the rules and task while end users supply only the inputs. Giving the developer's instructions precedence is what keeps user text from simply rewriting how the application behaves.

questions.t: In a Markov decision process (MDP), the next state and reward depend only on the current state and action, so the state must summarise everything relevant about the past.
questions.f: In a Markov decision process (MDP), the next state and reward depend on the full history of states and actions, so the agent must remember everything about the past.
questions.x: The Markov property is what makes MDPs tractable: the current state is a sufficient summary, so values and policies can be defined per state. When the agent cannot observe such a state, the problem becomes a partially observable MDP, where the agent tracks a belief over states instead.

questions.t: Cyril Cleverdon's Cranfield experiments in the 1960s set the template for evaluating information retrieval: a fixed document collection, a set of queries and human relevance judgments.
questions.f: Gerard Salton's SMART experiments in the 1960s set the template for evaluating information retrieval: a fixed document collection, a set of queries and human relevance judgments.
questions.x: Cleverdon ran the Cranfield tests at the Cranfield College of Aeronautics from 1958 to 1966, and NIST's TREC later scaled the same collection-queries-judgments recipe up. Salton's SMART project is remembered for ranking ideas such as the vector space model and TF-IDF weighting, not for the evaluation template.

questions.t: An inverted index maps each term to a postings list of the documents that contain it, so answering a query only means reading the lists for the query's terms.
questions.f: An inverted index maps each document to a list of the terms it contains, so answering a query only means reading the lists for the query's terms.
questions.x: Scanning every document at query time is far too slow for large collections, so IR systems index in advance by term. Storing terms per document is the forward direction; the index is called inverted precisely because it flips that to documents per term.

questions.t: In 2020, Dense Passage Retrieval's dual encoder beat a strong Lucene BM25 baseline by 9 to 19 points absolute in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy on open-domain question answering.
questions.f: In 2020, a strong Lucene BM25 baseline beat Dense Passage Retrieval's dual encoder by 9 to 19 points absolute in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy on open-domain question answering.
questions.x: Karpukhin et al. encoded questions and passages separately into dense vectors, and that learned matching clearly outperformed keyword scoring on their QA benchmarks. The result helped shift IR toward neural retrievers, though BM25 stays the baseline every new retriever is measured against.

questions.t: An intrinsic hallucination contradicts the source text, while an extrinsic hallucination can be neither supported nor refuted by the source.
questions.f: An extrinsic hallucination contradicts the source text, while an intrinsic hallucination can be neither supported nor refuted by the source.
questions.x: In Ji et al.'s taxonomy, a summary giving the wrong year for a dated event is intrinsic because the source shows it is wrong. An extrinsic addition might even be true, but nothing in the input lets you check it.

questions.t: Kalai and colleagues argue hallucinations persist after post-training partly because benchmarks score an abstention as zero, so a confident guess earns more on average.
questions.f: Kalai and colleagues argue hallucinations persist after post-training partly because benchmarks penalise an abstention below zero, so a confident guess earns more on average.
questions.x: Like a multiple-choice exam with no penalty for wrong answers, a guess sometimes scores while saying 'I don't know' never does, so models are pushed to bluff. Their proposed fix is to penalise confident errors more than abstentions in mainstream benchmarks, not to punish abstaining.

questions.t: Semantic entropy samples several answers to a question, groups them by meaning and measures entropy over those groups, so high entropy flags a likely confabulation.
questions.f: Semantic entropy samples several answers to a question, groups them by exact wording and measures entropy over those groups, so high entropy flags a likely confabulation.
questions.x: Grouping by meaning, using an entailment model or an LLM, stops differently worded but equivalent answers from looking like disagreement. The method costs roughly ten queries and cannot catch errors a model makes consistently, such as a fact it learned wrongly.

questions.t: Wei et al. at Google Research coined the term instruction tuning, while the concurrent BigScience paper by Sanh et al. called the same idea multitask prompted training.
questions.f: Sanh et al. at BigScience coined the term instruction tuning, while the concurrent Google Research paper by Wei et al. called the same idea multitask prompted training.
questions.x: Wei et al.'s FLAN paper (ICLR 2022) introduced the name and instruction-tuned Google's 137-billion-parameter LaMDA-PT. Sanh et al.'s T0 work at BigScience appeared at the same time under the label multitask prompted training, so the two names are often mixed up.

questions.t: To test zero-shot generalization, FLAN held out whole task clusters, so no natural language inference dataset was trained on when evaluating inference.
questions.f: To test zero-shot generalization, FLAN held out single datasets, so other natural language inference datasets were trained on when evaluating inference.
questions.x: Holding out a single dataset would let the model see the same kind of task in sibling datasets, which flatters zero-shot scores. Removing the entire cluster means the model has truly never been trained on that task type, so any gain shows instruction following carrying over to new tasks.

questions.t: In FLAN's experiments, instruction tuning improved the 68B and 137B models on unseen tasks but hurt held-out performance for models of 8B parameters or fewer.
questions.f: In FLAN's experiments, instruction tuning improved models of 8B parameters or fewer on unseen tasks but hurt held-out performance for the 68B and 137B models.
questions.x: So in the original FLAN setup the benefit appeared only at large scale. Later work with far more tasks (Chung et al.) reported gains for smaller models too, so the size threshold depends on the instruction-data mix rather than being fixed.

questions.t: In-context learning picks up a task from instructions or demonstrations placed in the prompt, within a forward pass and with the model's weights left unchanged.
questions.f: In-context learning picks up a task from instructions or demonstrations placed in the prompt, by taking a few gradient steps that update the model's weights.
questions.x: In-context learning changes only the input, never the parameters, which is what separates it from fine-tuning. That is why one deployed model can switch tasks just by changing its prompt, even though its training only ever asked it to predict the next token.

questions.t: An induction head is an attention circuit that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies the token that followed it.
questions.f: An induction head is an attention circuit that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies the token that preceded it.
questions.x: Copying what came next last time lets a model continue a pattern it has already seen in the prompt, a simple form of learning from context. Anthropic researchers linked these heads to in-context learning; copying the preceding token would not help predict what comes next.

questions.t: Von Oswald et al. built a linear self-attention layer whose output equals one gradient-descent step on a regression loss, a result shown only on simple regression tasks.
questions.f: Von Oswald et al. built a linear self-attention layer whose output equals one gradient-descent step on a regression loss, a result they confirmed directly in large pretrained language models.
questions.x: The construction suggests a transformer could in principle learn inside its forward pass the way an optimiser would. But it was demonstrated only on simple regression with self-attention-only models, so it is one candidate explanation of in-context learning, not a settled account of large LLMs.

questions.topic: Vision-language model: LLMs with visual input
questions.t: Flamingo scales each new cross-attention layer's output by tanh(α) with α initialised to zero, so at the start of training the model behaves exactly like its frozen language model.
questions.f: Flamingo scales each new cross-attention layer's output by tanh(α) with α initialised to one, so at the start of training visual features already dominate its frozen language model.
questions.x: Since tanh(0) is 0, the inserted layers start switched off and the pretrained LM's behaviour is preserved; the gate then opens gradually as α is learned. Starting the gate fully open would disrupt the frozen LM and make training unstable, which is what the zero init avoids.

questions.topic: Vision-language model: LLMs with visual input
questions.t: A 2023 study of object hallucination found vision-language models most often invent objects that are frequent in visual-instruction data or that commonly co-occur with objects really in the image.
questions.f: A 2023 study of object hallucination found vision-language models most often invent objects that are rare in visual-instruction data or that seldom co-occur with objects really in the image.
questions.x: Hallucinated objects follow the training statistics: the model fills in what usually appears or usually accompanies what it sees, not unusual objects. The same study proposed POPE, polling the model with yes/no questions about specific objects, because caption-based metrics were skewed by prompts and generation style.

questions.topic: Vision-language model: LLMs with visual input
questions.t: BLIP-2's authors reported in 2023 that it beat Flamingo-80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 while training 54 times fewer parameters, thanks to keeping its image encoder and LLM frozen.
questions.f: BLIP-2's authors reported in 2023 that it beat Flamingo-80B by 8.7% on zero-shot VQAv2 while training 5 times fewer parameters, thanks to keeping its image encoder and LLM frozen.
questions.x: BLIP-2 trains only a lightweight Querying Transformer (Q-Former) between a frozen image encoder and a frozen LLM, so its trainable parameter count is tiny: 54 times fewer than Flamingo-80B, not merely 5. It shows that a small learned bridge between big frozen models can be both cheap and strong.

questions.t: In 2023, GPT-4 as a judge agreed with human experts on 85% of non-tied MT-Bench votes, slightly above the 81% at which the experts agreed with one another.
questions.f: In 2023, GPT-4 as a judge agreed with human experts on 81% of non-tied MT-Bench votes, slightly below the 85% at which the experts agreed with one another.
questions.x: Zheng et al.'s headline finding was that a strong LLM judge matched human preferences about as well as humans match each other. That is why LLM judges are used as a cheap first pass, though they are still checked against samples of human ratings.

questions.t: G-Eval has the judge model first generate evaluation steps by chain-of-thought, then fill in a form with scores for criteria such as coherence or fluency.
questions.f: G-Eval has the judge model first fill in a form with scores for criteria such as coherence or fluency, then generate evaluation steps by chain-of-thought.
questions.x: Reasoning before scoring lets the judge decide what to check before it commits to a number; writing the reasoning afterwards would only justify a verdict already made. With GPT-4 as backbone, G-Eval correlated with human summary ratings well above earlier automatic metrics.

questions.t: To counter position bias, LLM judges are often run on both orders of the two answers, counting a win only when the verdict stays the same.
questions.f: To counter verbosity bias, LLM judges are often run on both orders of the two answers, counting a win only when the verdict stays the same.
questions.x: Position bias means a judge favours an answer because of where it sits; in Zheng et al.'s tests GPT-4 kept its verdict after a swap only 65% of the time. Swapping the order does nothing about verbosity bias, the pull toward longer, padded answers.

questions.t: AlphaZero trains its policy head to match the move distribution from tree-search visit counts and its value head to predict each self-play game's final result.
questions.f: AlphaZero trains its value head to match the move distribution from tree-search visit counts and its policy head to predict each self-play game's final result.
questions.x: The policy head outputs move probabilities, so it imitates the search's improved distribution; the value head outputs one number, so it regresses toward the game outcome z. Search proposes stronger moves than the raw network and the network learns to reproduce them, so each round of self-play starts from a better player.

questions.t: In DeepMind's 2018 evaluation, AlphaZero searched about 60,000 chess positions per second, against roughly 60 million for Stockfish.
questions.f: In DeepMind's 2018 evaluation, AlphaZero searched about 60 million chess positions per second, against roughly 60,000 for Stockfish.
questions.x: AlphaZero searched about a thousand times fewer positions than Stockfish and still won, because its learned evaluation guided a much smaller, more selective search. It was the classical engine that relied on brute-force breadth.

questions.t: AlphaZero must be given a game's rules to search ahead, limiting it to domains with known dynamics, whereas MuZero later planned with a model it learned itself.
questions.f: MuZero must be given a game's rules to search ahead, limiting it to domains with known dynamics, whereas AlphaZero later planned with a model it learned itself.
questions.x: AlphaZero's tree search needs a perfect simulator, which is why it was confined to board games. MuZero, the later system, replaced the rules with a learned model, matching AlphaZero in Go, chess and shogi while also handling Atari games.

questions.t: In function calling the model never runs a tool itself: it emits a tool name and arguments matching a declared schema, and the application or provider executes the call.
questions.f: In function calling the model runs the tool itself during generation, using the code behind each declared schema, and the application only receives the final answer.
questions.x: The model sees only each tool's name, description and JSON Schema, never its code, so all it can do is ask; the host executes the call and feeds the result back for the model to continue. That split is why permission checks belong in the application.

questions.t: AI21 Labs' 2022 MRKL paper proposed a router that sends each input to the most suitable expert module, neural or symbolic such as a calculator, with the language model as fallback.
questions.f: Meta AI's 2022 MRKL paper proposed a router that sends each input to the most suitable expert module, neural or symbolic such as a calculator, with the language model as fallback.
questions.x: MRKL (Modular Reasoning, Knowledge and Language) came from AI21 Labs, the maker of Jurassic-1, and argued that models lack fresh data and reliable arithmetic, so those jobs should go to external modules. Its hand-built router preceded models that choose tools themselves.

questions.t: In 2024 the Gorilla paper reported about 72% zero-shot accuracy on Hugging Face API calls for its fine-tuned LLaMA-7B, against about 20% for GPT-4.
questions.f: In 2024 the Gorilla paper reported about 20% zero-shot accuracy on Hugging Face API calls for its fine-tuned LLaMA-7B, against about 72% for GPT-4.
questions.x: Gorilla was fine-tuned on APIBench with retrieved API documentation in its prompts, so a small specialised model beat a far larger general one at producing correct calls, checked by abstract-syntax-tree matching. The false statement swaps the two scores.

questions.t: The Logic Theorist, often called the first AI program, was written in 1955–1956 by Allen Newell, J. C. Shaw and Herbert A. Simon at the RAND Corporation.
questions.f: The Logic Theorist, often called the first AI program, was written in 1955–1956 by Allen Newell, J. C. Shaw and Herbert A. Simon at Dartmouth College.
questions.x: Newell, Shaw and Simon built it at RAND, with funding mainly from the US Air Force, and a version ran on RAND's JOHNNIAC computer. Dartmouth is the tempting wrong answer because the program was coded around the time of the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.

questions.t: The Logic Theorist worked backward from the goal theorem, generating subproblems whose solution would yield it, instead of enumerating every possible derivation.
questions.f: The Logic Theorist worked forward from the axioms, enumerating every possible derivation until the goal theorem appeared, instead of generating subproblems.
questions.x: Blind enumeration is what its authors called the British Museum algorithm, and they used it as the contrast. LT instead pruned the search with heuristics, working back from the goal and hunting for matching substitutions, a goal-directed style that became standard in automated reasoning.

questions.t: Hao Wang showed a complete, efficient propositional procedure easily proved the Principia theorems that had stumped the Logic Theorist.
questions.f: Hao Wang showed a complete, efficient propositional procedure stalled on the same Principia theorems that had stumped the Logic Theorist.
questions.x: Wang's result undercut the suggestion that exhaustive enumeration was the only alternative to heuristics, since a systematic method did better. Martin Davis replied that efficient proving was never LT's aim; it was meant to model human problem solving.

questions.topic: Model serving: deploying trained models behind inference APIs
questions.t: Clipper's adaptive batching used an additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease rule to find the largest batch size that still met its latency objective.
questions.f: Clipper's adaptive batching used a multiplicative-increase, additive-decrease rule to find the largest batch size that still met its latency objective.
questions.x: Growing the batch slowly and cutting it sharply when a latency target such as 20 ms is missed lets the server probe for throughput without long latency violations. The false version reverses the rule, which would overshoot the target quickly and recover slowly.

questions.topic: Model serving: deploying trained models behind inference APIs
questions.t: In TensorFlow-Serving, an availability-preserving policy loads a new model version before unloading the old one, while a resource-preserving policy unloads the old one first.
questions.f: In TensorFlow-Serving, a resource-preserving policy loads a new model version before unloading the old one, while an availability-preserving policy unloads the old one first.
questions.x: Keeping the old version up until the new one is ready means the model never goes offline, but briefly needs memory for two copies. When two copies will not fit, the resource-preserving policy accepts a short gap instead; the false statement swaps the two policies.

questions.topic: Model serving: deploying trained models behind inference APIs
questions.t: In 2017 Google's TensorFlow-Serving authors estimated that the serving library alone could handle about 100,000 requests per second per CPU core.
questions.f: In 2017 Google's TensorFlow-Serving authors estimated that the serving library alone could handle about 10,000 requests per second per CPU core.
questions.x: The estimate covers only the serving framework's own overhead, not model computation, and shows the plumbing is rarely the bottleneck. The false figure is ten times too low; Google's total traffic then ran to tens of millions of inferences per second.

questions.t: Elman's 1990 simple recurrent network fed a copy of the previous hidden-layer activations back in through context units, alongside the current input.
questions.f: Elman's 1990 simple recurrent network fed a buffer of the most recent raw inputs back in as an extra spatial dimension, alongside the current input.
questions.x: Elman argued that treating time as an extra spatial dimension fixes the pattern length and treats shifted copies of a pattern as different. His network represented time implicitly through recycled hidden state, the core idea of an RNN's hidden state.

questions.t: In a gated recurrent unit (GRU), the reset gate sets how much past state feeds the new candidate, while the update gate sets how much old state is carried forward.
questions.f: In a gated recurrent unit (GRU), the update gate sets how much past state feeds the new candidate, while the reset gate sets how much old state is carried forward.
questions.x: The two gates are easy to swap: reset shapes the candidate state, update blends old and new state. Such gates, deciding what to keep and what to overwrite, are how gated RNNs counter vanishing gradients, and the GRU is a lighter alternative to the LSTM.

questions.t: Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio (ICML 2013) proposed clipping the gradient norm to tame exploding gradients in RNNs, and a soft regularisation constraint for vanishing ones.
questions.f: Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio (ICML 2013) proposed clipping the gradient norm to tame vanishing gradients in RNNs, and a soft regularisation constraint for exploding ones.
questions.x: Clipping caps a gradient that has grown too large, so it cannot rescue one that has shrunk towards zero. Both problems come from multiplying through the same recurrent weights many times in backpropagation through time; vanishing gradients are better fixed by gated architectures.

questions.t: US executive orders on AI bind only the executive branch, cannot override statutes, and can be revoked by the next President.
questions.f: US executive orders on AI bind private developers as well as agencies, override conflicting statutes, and can be revoked only by Congress.
questions.x: An executive order is an instruction from the President to federal agencies, so its reach over companies comes only through follow-on rules, guidance and procurement terms. That is also why it is fragile: a new President can rescind it, as happened to EO 14110 within days in January 2025.

questions.t: EO 13859, signed in February 2019, launched the American AI Initiative and set five guiding principles for US federal AI policy.
questions.f: EO 14110, signed in February 2019, launched the American AI Initiative and set five guiding principles for US federal AI policy.
questions.x: EO 13859 was an early AI-focused order; its principles covered research, technical standards, workforce training, public trust and protecting US technological advantage. EO 14110 came later, in October 2023, and was far broader, with eight guiding principles and tasks for dozens of agencies.

questions.t: EO 14110 tied mandatory developer reporting to fixed training-compute thresholds, whereas EO 14409 relies on voluntary government access and a classified capability test.
questions.f: EO 14110 relied on voluntary government access and a classified capability test, whereas EO 14409 tied mandatory developer reporting to fixed training-compute thresholds.
questions.x: The 2023 order used the Defense Production Act to require reports from developers above set compute levels. The 2026 order instead has the NSA designate covered frontier models by benchmarking advanced cyber capabilities, and explicitly creates no mandatory licensing, leaving open which yardstick for frontier risk will last.

questions.t: By late 2026 TensorRT-LLM ran models as native PyTorch code and loaded Hugging Face checkpoints directly, having removed its step of compiling a TensorRT engine ahead of time.
questions.f: By late 2026 TensorRT-LLM compiled every model into a TensorRT engine ahead of time with trtllm-build, having removed its PyTorch backend.
questions.x: TensorRT-LLM began as an engine-compiling workflow, added a PyTorch backend as a beta in version 0.17, then made PyTorch its sole execution backend and dropped trtllm-build. Despite the name, older tutorials' engine-build step no longer exists, so the false statement has the change backwards.

questions.t: TensorRT-LLM's FP8 quantization needs Hopper-generation or later NVIDIA GPUs, while its FP4 formats need Blackwell GPUs such as the B200.
questions.f: TensorRT-LLM's FP4 quantization needs Hopper-generation or later NVIDIA GPUs, while its FP8 formats need Blackwell GPUs such as the B200.
questions.x: Low-precision formats depend on tensor-core hardware support, so each new format arrives with a GPU generation: FP8 with Hopper (H100) and FP4 with Blackwell. This tie to specific NVIDIA hardware is the library's main lock-in; the false statement swaps the two generations.

questions.t: In September 2023 NVIDIA reported that H100 GPUs running TensorRT-LLM gave up to 8 times the GPT-J-6B summarization throughput of A100 GPUs.
questions.f: In September 2023 NVIDIA reported that H100 GPUs running TensorRT-LLM gave up to 8 times the GPT-J-6B summarization throughput of H100 GPUs without it.
questions.x: The baseline was an older GPU generation, so the 8x mixes a hardware upgrade with software gains and does not isolate what the library adds. The false version makes it a same-hardware comparison, which is exactly the reading a vendor benchmark like this does not support.

questions.t: The name retrieval-augmented generation comes from a 2020 NeurIPS paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues, whose generator drew on a dense vector index of Wikipedia.
questions.f: The name retrieval-augmented generation comes from a 2020 ICML paper by Kelvin Guu and colleagues, whose generator drew on a dense vector index of Wikipedia.
questions.x: Lewis et al. coined RAG, pairing a seq2seq model's parametric memory with a non-parametric Wikipedia index. Guu et al.'s REALM, at ICML 2020, was the precursor: it added a retriever to masked-language-model pretraining but extracted answers rather than generating them.

questions.t: RAG-Sequence conditions the whole answer on one retrieved passage at a time, while RAG-Token can draw on a different retrieved passage for each generated token.
questions.f: RAG-Token conditions the whole answer on one retrieved passage at a time, while RAG-Sequence can draw on a different retrieved passage for each generated token.
questions.x: Both variants treat the retrieved passages as a latent variable and marginalise over them; they differ in where the sum sits. RAG-Sequence sums over passages for the full output, while RAG-Token sums at every token, letting one answer combine evidence from several passages.

questions.t: Compared with fine-tuning, RAG makes knowledge easy to update and answers traceable to sources, while fine-tuning gives more control over style and format and lower latency.
questions.f: Compared with fine-tuning, RAG gives more control over style and format and lower latency, while fine-tuning makes knowledge easy to update and answers traceable to sources.
questions.x: Swapping documents in an index updates what a RAG system knows without retraining, and the retrieved passages show where an answer came from, but the retrieval step adds latency. Fine-tuning bakes behaviour into the weights, which suits style and format, so the two are often combined.

questions.topic: Pretraining: learning general-purpose representations before task adaptation
questions.t: BERT's masked language modelling picks about 15% of input tokens, mostly replaces them with a mask symbol, and trains the model to recover them from context on both sides.
questions.f: BERT's masked language modelling picks about 15% of input tokens, mostly replaces them with a mask symbol, and trains the model to recover them from the left context only.
questions.x: Masking lets an encoder look both ways while still having a target to predict, which is why BERT is bidirectional. Predicting from left context only is causal language modelling, the objective of GPT-style decoders.

questions.topic: Pretraining: learning general-purpose representations before task adaptation
questions.t: Erhan, Bengio and colleagues argued that unsupervised pretraining helps deep networks mainly as a regularizer, steering them toward parameters that generalise better.
questions.f: Erhan, Bengio and colleagues argued that unsupervised pretraining helps deep networks mainly as an optimizer, steering them toward parameters that fit the training set better.
questions.x: Their experiments varying depth, capacity and data size pointed to better generalisation rather than easier fitting, so they framed pretraining as a kind of regularization. The account opened, but did not settle, the question of why pretraining transfers so well.

questions.topic: Pretraining: learning general-purpose representations before task adaptation
questions.t: In 2024 Meta reported pretraining its 405-billion-parameter Llama 3 model on about 15.6 trillion tokens.
questions.f: In 2024 Meta reported pretraining its 405-billion-parameter Llama 3 model on about 1.56 trillion tokens.
questions.x: That is roughly 38 tokens per parameter and about 3.8 x 10^25 FLOPs of compute, versus about 3.3 billion words for BERT-large. The jump shows how pretraining scaled up data, not only parameters, after Chinchilla showed many big models were undertrained.

questions.t: Underfitting shows up as high error on both training and validation data with only a small gap between them, usually because the model is too simple.
questions.f: Underfitting shows up as high error on both training and validation data with only a small gap between them, usually because the model is too complex.
questions.x: An underfit model cannot capture the pattern even on data it has seen, so both errors stay high. Excess complexity causes the opposite problem, overfitting, where training error is low but validation error is much higher.

questions.t: On a generalization curve, overfitting appears when training loss keeps falling or levels off while validation loss turns upward.
questions.f: On a generalization curve, overfitting appears when validation loss keeps falling or levels off while training loss turns upward.
questions.x: Plotting both losses against training iterations is the standard diagnostic: the model keeps improving on data it has memorized while getting worse on held-out data. Training loss rising while validation loss falls is not the overfitting signature.

questions.t: Caruana, Lawrence and Giles (NIPS 2000) found oversized networks trained by backpropagation with early stopping generalized well, while conjugate gradient tended to overfit.
questions.f: Caruana, Lawrence and Giles (NIPS 2000) found oversized networks trained by conjugate gradient with early stopping generalized well, while backpropagation tended to overfit.
questions.x: They explained that networks of different sizes learn a task's subcomponents in a similar order, so with early stopping a big backprop-trained network can match a smaller one. Conjugate gradient was the method they found prone to overfitting smooth regions of the input space.

questions.t: Min et al. (EMNLP 2022) found that swapping the gold labels in demonstrations for random ones barely hurt accuracy across 12 models, including GPT-3.
questions.f: Min et al. (EMNLP 2022) found that swapping the gold labels in demonstrations for random ones sharply cut accuracy across 12 models, including GPT-3.
questions.x: Demonstrations mostly show the model the label space, the kind of input text and the output format, not the correct input-label mapping. That is why few-shot examples are good at controlling format and weak at teaching genuinely new knowledge.

questions.t: Liu et al. found that retrieving demonstrations semantically similar to each test query, using a sentence encoder, consistently beat randomly chosen examples for GPT-3.
questions.f: Liu et al. found that randomly chosen demonstrations consistently beat examples retrieved for semantic similarity to each test query, using a sentence encoder, for GPT-3.
questions.x: Which examples go in the prompt matters, and nearby examples help most. This turned example selection into a retrieval problem: production systems keep a pool of labelled cases and pull each query's nearest neighbours into the prompt.

questions.t: In the 2020 GPT-3 paper, few-shot prompts typically held 10 to 100 demonstrations, capped by what fit in the model's 2,048-token context window.
questions.f: In the 2020 GPT-3 paper, few-shot prompts typically held 10 to 100 demonstrations, capped by what fit in the model's 32,768-token context window.
questions.x: The number of demonstrations is bounded by the context window, and GPT-3's was only 2,048 tokens. Much longer windows later made many-shot prompting with hundreds or thousands of examples possible.

questions.t: AI safety is broader than AI alignment: alignment asks whether a system pursues what its designers intend, while safety also covers misuse and failures on unusual inputs.
questions.f: AI alignment is broader than AI safety: safety asks whether a system pursues what its designers intend, while alignment also covers misuse and failures on unusual inputs.
questions.x: A perfectly aligned system can still be misused by its operator, break on out-of-distribution inputs or cause harm once deployed widely, and those problems belong to safety. That is why alignment is treated as one part of AI safety, not the other way round.

questions.t: Hendrycks and colleagues' 2021 paper Unsolved Problems in ML Safety split the field into four problems: robustness, monitoring, alignment and systemic safety.
questions.f: Amodei and colleagues' 2016 paper Concrete Problems in AI Safety split the field into four problems: robustness, monitoring, alignment and systemic safety.
questions.x: The 2021 roadmap framed safety around hazards: withstanding them, detecting them, reducing those inside the model and reducing those in the wider system. The 2016 Concrete Problems paper instead framed the field as preventing accidents and listed five problems such as reward hacking and safe exploration.

questions.t: The 2025 International AI Safety Report found broad agreement that current systems cannot cause loss of control, but real disagreement on its likelihood over the next several years.
questions.f: The 2025 International AI Safety Report found broad agreement that loss of control is likely over the next several years, but real disagreement on whether current systems could cause it.
questions.x: The experts converged on today's systems lacking the capability, and split on how fast that could change. This uncertainty feeds the report's evidence dilemma: acting early on thin evidence may prove unnecessary, while waiting may leave society unprepared.

questions.t: Cheng, Dong and Lapata's Long Short-Term Memory-Network (EMNLP 2016) was an early form of self-attention, scoring each token against all earlier hidden states.
questions.f: Cheng, Dong and Lapata's Long Short-Term Memory-Network (EMNLP 2019) was an early form of self-attention, scoring each token against all earlier hidden states.
questions.x: Attention between two sequences came first; attending within one sequence emerged around 2016, a year before the Transformer. The LSTMN replaced the LSTM's single memory cell with a tape of one vector per earlier token, so 2019 is too late to be a precursor.

questions.t: Self-attention on its own ignores token order: shuffling the input tokens just shuffles the outputs the same way, so order must be added with positional encodings.
questions.f: Self-attention on its own captures token order: shuffling the input tokens changes every output, so positional encodings are an optional extra.
questions.x: Each output is a weighted sum over all tokens, and the weights depend only on content, not position. Without positional encodings, learned or sinusoidal, a transformer would see a sentence as a bag of tokens.

questions.t: Jain and Wallace (NAACL 2019) found attention weights often correlate poorly with gradient-based importance, and quite different attention patterns can give the same prediction.
questions.f: Jain and Wallace (NAACL 2019) found attention weights closely track gradient-based importance, and quite different attention patterns always change the prediction.
questions.x: If very different attention maps can produce the same output, a map cannot be taken as the reason for that output. Their result is why raw attention heatmaps should not be read as faithful explanations of model behaviour.

questions.t: A linear classifier on CIFAR-10 flattens each 32×32×3 image into 3,072 numbers, so its weight matrix W is 10×3,072 and yields one score per class.
questions.f: A linear classifier on CIFAR-10 flattens each 32×32×3 image into 1,024 numbers, so its weight matrix W is 10×1,024 and yields one score per class.
questions.x: Each colour image has 32 × 32 pixels times 3 channels, giving 3,072 inputs; 1,024 would count only one channel. Each of W's 10 rows acts as a template for one class, scored against the whole flattened image as f(x, W) = Wx + b.

questions.t: The ImageNet challenge (ILSVRC) scored classifiers by top-5 error, allowing five guesses per image because photos often contain several objects while only one is labeled.
questions.f: The ImageNet challenge (ILSVRC) scored classifiers by top-5 error, allowing five guesses per image because each photo was labeled with five correct object categories.
